坦布里察琴屬弦鳴樂器，發聲靠彈撥成對或單根琴弦。舊式琴身曾由整段木料挖鑿成梨形，: The tamburica is a chordophone sounded by plucking paired or single strings. Older bodies were carved from a single piece of wood in a pear shape; later most were built with a glued soundbox in the manner of a guitar. The neck carries movable or fixed frets, and the headstock was early pointed, later sometimes a scroll. Historical accounts give gut strings rather than metal; the bass instruments have a shorter bridge, with the strings parallel to the body, and the sound hole may be violin-style or round. Sources do not record the materials of the remaining parts.
坦布里察琴屬弦鳴樂器，發聲靠撥弦，弦常成雙且同度調音；品絲可移動，以利演奏不同調: The tamburica is a chordophone sounded by plucking; the strings are usually paired and tuned in unison, and the frets can be moved, which helps in playing different modes. The source gives no complete method, but the family division of labour covers the basics: the prim mostly leads the melody or plays harmony; the bugarija has four single strings and mostly strums chords off the beat to keep rhythm; the čelo plays bass notes and no chords; the bas is the largest, played standing for a bass line, or seated on a bar stool or double-bass chair so that the body rests against the belly. On gut-strung versions the string passes through a small hole in the neck and is tied behind it.

Ensembles run from a trio to a large tamburica orchestra; the basic trio uses prim, kontra and čelo, and larger line-ups add bass instruments such as the basprim. Osijek holds a tamburica festival every year.

The tamburica is a group of chordophones in the long-necked lute family, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321. Its strings are mostly paired and it is played by plucking; the frets on the neck can be moved, which makes different modes easy to play. It is widespread in the Balkans, especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Hungary, Montenegro, Serbia and Slovenia; in Croatia and Serbia it is a national string instrument, and it is also found in Vojvodina, Mačva, Posavo-Tamnava, and in the Croatian and Hungarian communities of Burgenland in Austria. Ensembles range from a trio to a large orchestra.
坦布里察琴為長頸魯特琴家族，名稱與部分特徵源自波斯坦布爾琴，流行於巴爾幹。其進入: The tamburica belongs to the long-necked lute family; its name and some of its features come from the tanbur, and it is widespread in the Balkans. Reliable information on how it reached Central Europe is thin; related instruments existed in Byzantine times, and the ancient Greek pandouris is counted as one of its ancestors. At the end of the nineteenth century, people in Serbia and Croatia developed the several forms known today. The earliest documented instrument still in existence is in Osijek from 1847, owned by Pajo Kolarić, who also founded the first amateur tamburica orchestra. After 1875, refugees brought gut-strung instruments to Sremski Karlovci; the carpenter Josip rebuilt them in a small-guitar shape, and in 1877 or 1878 Joza built a bass instrument. The modern forms and tunings were settled in Budapest between 1900 and the first half of the 1910s, and then passed into traditional ensembles in several countries.
坦布里察琴音色明亮清脆，具有溫暖而富有穿透力的特質。作為長頸琵琶樂器，其音域跨越: The tamburica has a bright, clear timbre, warm and able to carry. As a long-necked lute its range spans the middle and upper register, and its tone sits between the guitar and the mandolin, with a light, springy feel. Its particular resonance comes from the round or pear-shaped soundbox, so the tone is neither as heavy and deep as a classical guitar nor as hard and piercing as a pipa; it balances warmth with edge. The many strings give rich overtones and a clearly layered sound. In folk bands the tamburica often carries the harmony; its well-defined, grainy tone blends into the texture and still brings out a distinct local colour.
